data.title: Gold's biggest risk may not be a price crash. It's what happens afterwards
data.description:
Gold prices continued their sharp decline on Friday, November 20, with domestic gold futures for December 4 delivery opening 3.94 percent lower at Rs 1,22,430 per 10 grams on the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX). Bullion prices hovered near their lowest levels since August 2025, pressured by a stronger US dollar, higher bond yields and expectations of tighter US monetary policy.

For investors watching their gold investments lose value, the immediate question is whether prices will recover. But history suggests there is another question worth asking: How long could that recovery take?

Gold has experienced several major corrections in the past. And while prices eventually recovered, investors who bought near the peaks sometimes had to wait almost a decade just to get back to their original purchase price.

What if you bought gold at the wrong time?

Historical data compiled by FundsIndia Research highlights three such episodes.

An investor buying near the 1980 peak would have waited almost 10 years for gold to regain that level in 1989.

A similar pattern emerged after the February 1996 peak. Gold did not recover to those levels until 2002, more than six years later.

The pattern repeated after November 2012. Gold took until June 2019, roughly six and a half years, to return to its previous peak.

These were three different market cycles, but they highlight the same problem: An investment can eventually recover while remaining disappointing for someone who needs the money sooner.

The problem isn't always the loss

Imagine investing Rs 1 lakh in gold and watching its value decline. You decide not to sell, expecting prices to recover.

Seven years later, your investment is finally worth Rs 1 lakh again. You have recovered your original investment, but you haven't earned anything in nominal terms, even before accounting for expenses.

Inflation makes that wait more expensive. The same Rs 1 lakh would buy less after seven years, meaning the investor has lost purchasing power despite recovering the original amount.

There is also the question of timing. If the money was meant for a wedding, a house purchase or another financial goal, waiting several years for gold to recover may not be practical.

What does this mean for gold investors today?

These historical episodes do not mean the current correction will take another seven or ten years to recover. Nor do they represent every gold investor's experience.

Someone who invested after prices had already corrected could have earned very different returns.

Gold can still serve as a portfolio diversifier, particularly during periods of uncertainty. However, its safe-haven reputation does not guarantee quick recovery or protection against short-term losses.

The bigger lesson from these historical cycles is that the price at which investors enter matters, but so does the time they can afford to remain invested.

Gold may eventually recover from a correction. The real question is whether an investor's financial plans can accommodate the wait.

data.title: Mistral Increases Asia Investment as Sovereign AI Deals Grow — Interview
data.description:
By Kimberley Kao

French artificial-intelligence startup Mistral is boosting its investments in Asia as it expands its footprint in a region to meet swelling demand for sovereign AI.

The company plans to open new offices in South Korea and India "as soon as possible" within the next year, as it boosts its regional investment beyond dozens of millions of dollars, Mistral Chief Revenue Officer Marjorie Janiewicz and Vice-President of Revenue in Asia Geoff Soon said in a joint interview Friday.

"Over the past two to three years, we've seen a great acceleration of interest for Mistral in Asia Pacific," Janiewicz said. "We expect a lot of growth and return on that significant investment we're making in the region," she said.

The company has seen "explosive" demand from South Korea, Soon said.

The comments came as Mistral launched its regional headquarters in Singapore, saying it aims to more than double its Asia-Pacific headcount to 200 by 2027. Its investments will help accelerate the development, training and real-world deployment of sovereign AI models, it said.

Sovereign AI refers to a country's or organization's ability to develop and deploy its own AI infrastructure, as well as regulate and manage data used, rather than rely on external providers.

Mistral generates returns by licensing its core technology, working directly with customers with their AI deployment, and providing access to AI infrastructure, said Soon.

The company, which was recently valued above $24 billion after completing a new funding round led by South Korea's Samsung Electronics, aims to capture swelling demand for sovereign AI among governments and regulated businesses.

Contract values for the deployment of sovereign AI has been growing, she said.

"Because we are very focused on the right set of use case, customizing model and deploying them where those companies need, we see a fast conversion from proof of value to multi-use-case contract," Janiewicz said.

Demand has been coming from customers both in the private sector as well as government agencies which increasingly want to protect sensitive data while avoiding the steep token costs by using specialized task-specific AI models, Janiewicz said.

Mistral recently launched an open-weight AI model that Janiewicz said was done at the fraction of the compute costs compared with some U.S. players, with the cost savings passed down to customers.

"The fact that we can take our really strong general purpose models and distill them and fine tune them down to specialized models to drive efficiency and performance is really what's differentiating us," Soon said.

Write to Kimberley Kao at kimberley.kao@wsj.com

data.title: U.K. Government Borrowed More in October, But Stays on Track for Smaller Deficit — Update
data.description:
By Paul Hannon

The U.K. government borrowed more in October than a year earlier, but it remained on course to reduce its budget deficit in the current fiscal year.

The Office for National Statistics on Friday said government spending exceeded revenues by 17 billion pounds ($22.25 billion) in October, an increase of 800 million pounds from the same month of 2025.

The increase in borrowing partly reflected a rise in interest costs as inflation and bond yields picked up since the start of the war between the U.S. and Iran.

In October, interest payments totaled 11.2 billion pounds, an increase of 2.8 billion pounds from the same month last year.

"Much of the deficit is out of the government's control, with the war in the Middle East continuing to put pressure on inflation and the economy," said Kit Rees, an investment strategist at Quilter.

Over the first seven months of the fiscal year that will end in early April, borrowing was 111.3 billion pounds, down 7.3 billion pounds from the same period a year earlier.

At 3.5% of gross domestic product, the budget deficit for the fiscal year to October was lower than the 3.8% recorded a year earlier.

The government's total debt stood at 3.1 trillion pounds, or 95.8% of GDP, up from 93.9% in October 2025.

In its October budget, the government set out plans for spending and taxation that aim to reduce the budget deficit further in the current and subsequent fiscal years. However, borrowing is set to be higher than previously targeted.

For this year, the Office for Budget Responsibility estimates the budget deficit will be 4.2% of gross domestic product, a large increase from the 3.6% planned in March.

The overshoot partly reflects the increased costs of providing government services as energy prices have risen since the start of the war. Higher prices are also raising the cost of paying interest, since the U.K. has a higher share of bonds with payouts linked to inflation than its peers.

Write to Paul Hannon at paul.hannon@wsj.com

data.title: Anthropic Is Public — Is OpenAI Ready To Follow?
data.description:
Key points:
  • Commentators say the AI race isn't decided yet, though they praise Anthropic’s early focus on enterprise customers.
  • Vinod Khosla said token volume is a better metric to track leadership than revenue.
  • Anthropic’s stock rose 17% on its opening day after a blockbuster IPO.

On its path to an IPO, Anthropic, founded by former OpenAI employees, has outpaced the ChatGPT maker in sales and valuation, while pulling ahead in the race to become the first pure-play AI company to go public.

While investors will closely watch Anthropic’s market performance for a clearer view of leadership, commentators said the AI race is not decided yet.

OpenAI has not disclosed its financials, and available reports offer only a partial picture of its business, making a direct comparison with Anthropic difficult. However, some investors have praised its first-mover advantage, deep consumer penetration, compute investment, and competitive token prices as moats.

OpenAI vs Anthropic

OpenAI filed confidentially for the IPO before Anthropic, but by mid-2026 decided to defer the plan to next year amid reports that its revenue had fallen behind Anthropic’s.

As per The Information, OpenAI clocked $10 billion in sales in the third quarter, with $6.7 billion in Q2 and $5.7 billion in Q1. In comparison, Anthropic made $17 billion in sales, taking its revenue in the first nine months to $33.24 billion, nearly $11 billion more than OpenAI’s.

On the valuation front, OpenAI's latest private market valuation is $1.27 trillion, according to Nasdaq Private Market. Anthropic’s market capitalization swelled to $1.8 trillion after its strong debut on Thursday.

OpenAI also appears to be losing steam with users. Sensor Tower data shows Claude downloads in India jumped over 15-fold year over year, while ChatGPT downloads fell 21%. India is the biggest market for both companies.

OpenAI Investor Vinod Khosla Says Watch Tokens, Not Revenue

In a recent interview, storied investor and one of OpenAI's earliest backers, Vinod Khosla, dismissed Anthropic’s sales lead over the ChatGPT maker as a short-term metric and pitched token volume as the true indicator of long-term leadership.

“AI race is not what's happening quarter over quarter What's the trajectory over the next 2, 3, 5 years and what will be the situation in 2030 and beyond that,” Khosla said.

He said he believes OpenAI’s heavy R&D focus, compute investments and custom in-house silicon give it a cost advantage over rivals.

“I'm very happy with the kind of approach that OpenAI is taking. They have a large investment in R&D - probably the most research-oriented model company there is. They also have a large investment in compute which gives them a fundamental cost advantage. So to me revenue is not as important as measuring tokens."

He added that OpenAI has priced its tokens lower and “because of that it is growing share of tokens which is the intelligence and the service both of these companies are providing."

Khosla Ventures was the first VC investor in OpenAI, investing $50 million in 2018-19.

Dan Niles Praises Anthropic’s Enterprise Focus

In an analysis of the Anthropic IPO, Niles Investment Management founder Dan Niles praised the company’s early focus on enterprise vis-a-vis OpenAI.

“Anthropic was focused on day one on enterprises who are willing to pay vs OpenAI that focused on consumers who are used to getting internet services for free like search,” Niles said in an X post.

He added the Anthropic IPO would face over the next 30 days during the green shoe window.

Summarizing his analysis, Niles said price competition is increasing, rev growth is slowing, and operating margins are dropping for the two leading LLMs while capital commitments are massive.”

But “if I had to pick one LLM that survives the commoditization of this layer, Anthropic would be it. But it is not a favorite of mine for AI overall in the near-term.”

Anthropic IPO Recap, Stock Move

Anthropic sold 801.3 million shares, and selling shareholders sold 23.6 million shares in the IPO, raising a total of $107.3 billion, including $26 billion through a private placement.

ANT stock closed 17% higher on the first day, giving the company a market capitalization of roughly $1.8 trillion. However, shares tumbled 6.4% in overnight trading and weighed on tech stocks.

On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for ANT was ‘extremely bullish’ as of early Friday.

data.title: Retail sales spike after government urges households to stock up
data.description:
According to the Office for National Statistics, retail sales volumes jumped 0.7%, reversing September’s downwardly revised fall of 0.6%. Analysts had been expecting flat sales. Year-on-year, sales spiked 2.3%, comfortably ahead of expectations for a 1.7% rise.

Over the three months to October, the quantity of goods bought rose 0.4%, driven by higher volumes at food stores. Supermarkets reported increased sales of long-life items such as UHT milk and tinned goods following the Be Ready campaign, which urged households to stock up on basics, including bottled water, in case essential services unexpectedly went down.

Fuel sales also recovered, the ONS noted, despite pump prices rising again.

Erin Brookes, European retail and consumer lead at consultancy Alvarez & Marsal, said: “Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period.

“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs. With little scope to pass further increases onto shoppers, businesses face a difficult balancing act between offering compelling promotions and protecting already stretched margins. Black Friday will be a critical battleground.”

Separately, the ONS also published government debt figures on Friday, showing a 5.2% uplift year-on-year in public sector net borrowing in October, to £17bn. Consensus had been for £18bn.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year, with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly. However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly due to higher debt interest.”

data.title: Global investment banks see Chinese yuan's gradual appreciation extending into 2027
data.description:
Major global investment banks expect the Chinese yuan's gradual appreciation to extend into 2027, underpinned by resilient exports and a sizeable trade surplus.

While many analysts expect the central bank will continue to favour a measured appreciation, the People's Bank of China's (PBOC) decision this month to raise the amount of foreign currency financial institutions must hold as reserves may signal policymakers remain wary of excessively rapid rises.

The yuan has strengthened 4.8% against the dollar so far this year. The median forecast of six investment banks puts the currency at 6.44 per dollar by the end of 2027, implying a further 3.6% gain from Friday's 6.6691.

"China's current account and trade surpluses should remain strong in 2027. However, the PBOC has shifted towards resisting one-sided CNY appreciation. Without sustained expectations of further CNY gains, Chinese exporters have little incentive to accelerate USD selling."

** DEUTSCHE BANK

"We remain believers in the continued low-vol appreciation of the RMB. The continued policy push to expand RMB internationalization, political pressure from Europe for appreciation, and increasing domestic conversion of surpluses all support this trend."

** GOLDMAN SACHS

"Looking to next year, we expect more of the same — a booming export sector continuing to take global market share, and gradual but sustained appreciation towards fair value to keep protectionist pressures at bay from other jurisdictions."

** UBS

"A sizable current account surplus and easing capital outflow pressures should support the RMB. The PBOC may continue to allow market forces to drive the change and only step in when the pace is considered too rapid."

data.title: Europe before the bell: Selling not rotating
data.description:
EUROPE BEFORE THE BELL, SELLING NOT ROTATING

The stock market rotation is turning into outright selling with futures on the Euro Stoxx 50 down 1.6% after MSCI's broad APAC ex Japan index skidded 3%, leaving it set for its worst week since 2020.

Worries about the chip complex are at the heart of the selling, the Nikkei and KOSPI each fell over 5%, but the selling in Asia encompassed bourses with big representations from mining banks and old tech firms too.

The euro zone blue chip index is already down 4.2% since the start of the week, set for its worst week since March's 6.8% fall at the start of the US and Israeli war on Iran.

If we go through that, that takes us to the biggest weekly fall since April 2025's tariff drama.

The broad STOXX 600 milestones are similar.

But in Europe, the selling can't all be attributed to tech. Defensive like consumer staples (.SXCSP) and food and beverage (.SX3P) are each down over 3% on the week so far, as some traders don't just get out of tech, they get out of stocks.

The recent steep declines in metal prices is also weighing on miners.
